topics.name: Data Science Methodology
notes: **IBM's Data Science Methodology (John Rollins) — 10 stages**: 1 **Business Understanding** → 2 **Analytic Approach** → 3 **Data Requirements** → 4 **Data Collection** → 5 **Data Understanding** → 6 **Data Preparation** → 7 **Modeling** → 8 **Evaluation** → 9 **Deployment** → 10 **Feedback**. It is **iterative** (feedback loops back).

Guiding questions: Business understanding — "What is the problem you are trying to solve?"; Analytic approach — "How can you use data to answer the question?"; Data requirements — "What data do you need?"; Data collection — "Where is the data coming from and how will you get it?"; Data understanding — "Is the data representative of the problem?"; Data preparation — "What additional work is needed to manipulate the data?"; Modeling — "How can the data be visualised/modelled to get the answer?"; Evaluation — "Does the model answer the initial question?"; Deployment — "Can you put the model into practice?"; Feedback — "Can you get constructive feedback?"
**Data preparation** (cleaning, missing values, feature engineering) is usually the **most time-consuming** stage (often 70–80% of the effort).
Analytic approach types: **descriptive** (what is happening), **diagnostic** (why), **predictive** (what will happen), **prescriptive** (what should we do); classification for yes/no outcomes.
**CRISP-DM** (6 phases): Business understanding → Data understanding → Data preparation → Modeling → Evaluation → Deployment.

b: 2. Analytic approach — how can data answer it?
5. Data understanding · 6. Data preparation (takes the most time)

topics.name: Competing on Analytics (Internal & External Processes)
notes: **Competing on Analytics** (Thomas Davenport & Jeanne Harris, HBR 2006; book 2007): **analytical competitors** use sophisticated data analysis as a **key source of competitive advantage**, with enterprise-wide analytics and **strong senior-management support**.

**Internal processes**: **financial** analytics (performance management, scorecards), **M&A**, **operations/manufacturing** (quality, process optimisation), **R&D** (testing), **human resources / talent** analytics (e.g. Moneyball — Oakland A's).

**External processes**: **customer-facing** (CRM, segmentation, loyalty, pricing, marketing — Harrah's/Caesars, Capital One test-and-learn, Netflix recommendations, Progressive insurance pricing, Marriott revenue management) and **supplier-facing** (**supply chain** — Walmart Retail Link, UPS routing/ORION, Dell).
**Five stages of analytical competition**: 1 Analytically impaired → 2 Localised analytics → 3 Analytical aspirations → 4 Analytical companies → 5 **Analytical competitors**.
**DELTA model** for building analytical capability: **D**ata, **E**nterprise, **L**eadership, **T**argets, **A**nalysts.
Hallmarks of analytical competitors: analytics supports a **distinctive capability**, an **enterprise-wide** approach, **senior management commitment**, and **large-scale ambition**.

b: **Analytical competitors** use data as their main weapon, across the whole company, backed by top management.
Examples: Capital One (test & learn), Harrah's (loyalty), Netflix (recommendations), Walmart & UPS (supply chain), Oakland A's (Moneyball).
Five stages: Impaired → Localised → Aspirations → Analytical companies → **Analytical competitors**.

topics.name: Data Visualization & Analytics
notes: Choose the chart for the question: **Line** → trend over time. **Bar/column** → compare categories. **Histogram** → distribution of one numeric variable. **Scatter** → relationship/correlation between two numeric variables. **Box plot** → median, quartiles, spread and **outliers**. **Pie** → parts of a whole (few categories). **Heatmap** → matrix values, e.g. a correlation matrix.
Python: **Matplotlib** (plt.plot, plt.bar, plt.hist, plt.scatter, plt.boxplot), **Seaborn** (statistical plots: heatmap, pairplot, boxplot), Plotly (interactive). BI tools: Tableau, Power BI.
Good practice (Tufte): maximise the **data-ink ratio**, avoid chartjunk, label axes, start bar charts at zero (a **truncated axis can mislead**), use colour meaningfully.
Visual analytics helps explore data, find patterns/outliers, and communicate insights to stakeholders (dashboards, storytelling).

b: Label axes, start bars at zero (truncated axes mislead), remove clutter (high **data-ink ratio**).
Python: Matplotlib (plt.hist, plt.scatter) and Seaborn (pairplot, heatmap).

topics.name: Linear Regression for Business Analytics
notes: Regression predicts a **continuous** target (sales, price, demand). Simple: y = b₀ + b₁x; multiple: y = b₀ + Σbᵢxᵢ. Coefficients are found by **ordinary least squares** (minimise SSE).
**Interpretation**: b₁ = change in y per 1-unit increase in x (holding the others constant in multiple regression). b₀ = predicted y when all x = 0.
Fit quality: **R²**, adjusted R², RMSE; check **residual plots** (random scatter = good; patterns = misspecification), and use p-values for coefficient significance.
Python: `np.polyfit(x, y, 1)` returns [slope, intercept]; scikit-learn `LinearRegression().fit(X, y)` → `.coef_`, `.intercept_`, `.predict()`, `.score()` (R²). statsmodels OLS gives full summaries.
Normal equation: **b = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy**. Train/test split to check generalisation. Dummy (one-hot) variables encode categories.

b: Predict a number, e.g. Sales = 200 + 15 × AdSpend → AdSpend 10 → **350**.
The coefficient = change in Y per unit of X (holding the others fixed).
Check residual plots (patterns = a bad fit). Turn categories into **dummy variables**.

topics.name: Linear Optimization (Linear Programming)
notes: **LP**: optimise (max/min) a **linear objective** subject to **linear constraints** and non-negativity. Components: **decision variables**, **objective function**, **constraints**.
**Feasible region** = all points satisfying the constraints (a convex polygon in 2-D). **Corner-point theorem**: if an optimum exists, it occurs at a **vertex (corner point)** of the feasible region.
Graphical method (2 variables): plot the constraints, find the corners, evaluate the objective at each corner. Simplex method moves from vertex to vertex (for many variables).
Special cases: **infeasible** (no point satisfies all constraints), **unbounded** (objective can improve forever), **multiple optima** (objective parallel to a binding constraint).

**Slack** = unused amount of a ≤ constraint. **Binding constraint** = slack 0 at the optimum. **Shadow price (dual value)** = change in the optimal objective per one-unit increase in a constraint's RHS.
Python: **`scipy.optimize.linprog`** **minimises** by default → to maximise, minimise −c. Also PuLP. Applications: product mix, diet problem, transportation, scheduling, portfolio.

b: Choose amounts (**decision variables**) to maximise or minimise a linear **objective** under linear **constraints**.
💡 How many chairs and tables to make with limited wood and labour?
The best answer is always at a **corner** of the feasible region.
Max 3x + 2y with x + y ≤ 4, x + 3y ≤ 6: corners give 0, 12, 11, 4 → **12 at (4, 0)**.
- **Shadow price**: gain from one more unit of a resource
`scipy.optimize.linprog` **minimises** → negate to maximise. The simplex method hops between corners.

topics.name: Pandas Series
notes: **Series** = one-dimensional **labelled** array (values + **index**). Create from a list (default index 0..n−1), a **dict** (keys become the index), or a scalar with an index.
Access: `s['b']` / `s.loc['b']` by label, `s.iloc[0]` by position. Boolean filtering: `s[s > 15]`. Attributes: `.index`, `.values`, `.dtype`, `.size`, `.name`.
**Vectorised operations** (s * 2, s + 5). Arithmetic between two Series **aligns on the index**; labels present in only one Series give **NaN**.

Useful methods: `value_counts()` (frequency, sorted descending), `unique()`, `nunique()`, `isnull()/notnull()`, `fillna()`, `dropna()`, `describe()`, `apply()`, `map()`, `sort_values()`, `mean()` (skips NaN by default).
A DataFrame column is a Series: `df['col']`.

b: - From a dict: the keys become the index
- Adding two Series **lines up by index** → unmatched labels give **NaN**

topics.name: Pandas DataFrame
notes: **DataFrame** = 2-D labelled table (rows × columns); each column is a Series. `df.shape` → (rows, columns); `df.head()/tail()`, `df.info()`, **`df.describe()`** → count, mean, std, min, 25%, 50%, 75%, max.

Selection: `df['col']` (Series), `df[['c1','c2']]` (DataFrame). **`df.loc[rows, cols]`** = **label**-based and **slices include the end label**. **`df.iloc[rows, cols]`** = **position**-based and slices exclude the end. With a default index, `df.loc[0:2]` gives 3 rows, `df.iloc[0:2]` gives 2.
Filtering: `df[df['age'] > 30]`; combine conditions with `&` / `|` and parentheses.
**groupby**: `df.groupby('dept')['salary'].mean()` (split–apply–combine). `pivot_table`, `agg`.
Combining: **`pd.merge(df1, df2, on='id', how='inner'|'left'|'right'|'outer')`** (SQL-style joins); **`pd.concat([df1, df2])`** stacks rows (axis=0) or columns (axis=1); `df.join`.
Cleaning: `dropna()` (rows with NaN; axis=1 for columns), `fillna(value)`, `drop(columns=…)`, `rename`, `astype`, `drop_duplicates()`, `sort_values('col', ascending=False)`, `apply(func)`.

topics.name: Continuous & Discrete Probability Distributions
notes: **Discrete** (countable values, **PMF**): **Bernoulli** (one trial, p), **Binomial**(n, p) — mean **np**, variance **np(1 − p)**; **Poisson**(λ) — counts per interval, **mean = variance = λ**; **Geometric** — trials until the first success, mean 1/p; discrete uniform.

**Continuous** (**PDF**; P(X = exact value) = 0; probabilities are areas): **Uniform**[a, b] — mean (a + b)/2, variance (b − a)²/12; **Normal**(μ, σ) — symmetric bell; **Exponential**(λ) — time between events, mean 1/λ, **memoryless**; also t, chi-square, log-normal.
**Empirical rule** (normal): ~**68%** within 1σ, **95%** within 2σ, **99.7%** within 3σ. **z-score** = (x − μ)/σ; the standard normal has μ = 0, σ = 1.
**CDF** F(x) = P(X ≤ x). Expected value E[X] = Σx·p(x) (discrete) or ∫x·f(x)dx (continuous).
Python: `scipy.stats` (binom, poisson, norm, expon, uniform: .pmf/.pdf/.cdf), `np.random.normal/binomial/poisson`.
**Central Limit Theorem**: means of large samples are approximately normal, whatever the population's shape.

b: - **Binomial**(n, p): successes in n tries — mean np, variance np(1 − p)
- **Poisson**(λ): events per interval — mean = variance = λ
For continuous variables, P(X = exact value) = 0.
**Central Limit Theorem**: averages of large samples look normal.

topics.name: Exploratory Data Analysis
notes: **EDA** (John Tukey): explore data **before modelling** using summary statistics and visualisations to understand distributions, spot **outliers, missing values, errors**, relationships and patterns, and form hypotheses.

Steps: inspect structure (`shape`, `info`, `dtypes`, `head`), summary stats (`describe`), missing values (`isnull().sum()`), duplicates, univariate analysis (histograms, box plots), bivariate (scatter, correlation `df.corr()`, heatmaps), multivariate (pairplots).
**Central tendency**: mean (sensitive to outliers), median (robust), mode. **Spread**: range, variance, standard deviation, **IQR = Q3 − Q1**.
**Outliers by the IQR rule**: below **Q1 − 1.5·IQR** or above **Q3 + 1.5·IQR**. Also z-score > 3.
**Skewness**: right (positive) skew → long right tail, **mean > median**; left (negative) skew → mean < median; symmetric → mean ≈ median.
**Correlation ≠ causation**. Pearson r measures linear association; Spearman measures monotonic (rank) association.

b: Look at your data **before** modelling (John Tukey's idea): shape, missing values, outliers, relationships.
- Mean (pulled by outliers) vs **median** (robust) vs mode
- Outliers: below Q1 − 1.5·IQR or above Q3 + 1.5·IQR
- Histograms and box plots for one variable; scatter plots and heatmaps for pairs
- **Correlation ≠ causation** (ice cream and drowning share a cause: summer)
